title: The least of these (Matthew 25:31–46)
hook: a throne, every nation, and the King asks about bread, water, a coat and a visit
tomorrow: a whole jar of perfume poured out. waste, or something else?

segments.voice: Oil carried in before the wait, and a talent nobody buried: well done. Now the scene that ends the long teaching of Matthew 25.

A sandwich handed through a car window at a red light. A glass of water. A coat that doesn't fit you anymore. A hospital visit you almost skipped. Jesus sets those small things in front of a throne. "When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory." Every nation gathered, sorted like sheep and goats. And what does the King ask about? Bread, water, clothes, and visits.
screen: `A SANDWICH AT A RED LIGHT.` → `THE THRONE OF HIS GLORY.` → `HE ASKS ABOUT BREAD.`

segments.voice: The old question: where do you meet God? Here's the answer this scene gives. "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me." And the people are baffled. "Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee?" They never saw him at all. "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." The other side asks the same question and hears the same answer, turned over. Neither group knew. Christians read the least of these in more than one way: some hear everyone in need, some hear Jesus' own followers sent out with little. Now a neighbor. Muslims have a hadith, a saying the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reports from God, with the same surprise in it. On the Day of Resurrection, God says: son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit me. The person asks how anyone could visit the Lord of the worlds. And God answers: my servant was sick; had you visited him, you would have found me with him. Hunger and thirst come next, in the same pattern. So both traditions send you to a sickbed to find God. The honest difference: Christians hear Jesus the King saying the hungry stood in for him; Muslims hear God's nearness to the sick, and hold that God never becomes one of his creatures.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU MEET GOD?` · `HUNGRY, THIRSTY, A STRANGER, SICK.` · `NEITHER GROUP KNEW.` · `A NEIGHBOR: I WAS SICK.` · then, large: `YE HAVE DONE IT UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person easy to overlook: someone sick, alone, in prison, or new in town. Hold them gently, with no plan to fix anything yet. If you pray, you can hold them before God; if not, just let them stay in your thoughts a little longer than usual.
The least of these. The hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner, whom the King calls my brethren.
The line for today: you did it unto me, said to people who never saw him there. See you then.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching draws its corporal works of mercy from this list, and churches of different kinds run food pantries, clothing drives and prison visits in its spirit; some Christians visit care homes and hospitals as a regular practice.

notes: UNITY THREAD (wisdom day): the neighbor is a hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim 2569, paraphrased (no English translation quoted): God says on the Day of Resurrection, 'son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit me... had you visited him, you would have found me with him', then the same pattern for food and drink. A Muslim Keeper should confirm the paraphrase, the reference number, and that 'a saying the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reports from God' describes a hadith qudsi fairly.

Honest difference as voiced: 'Christians hear Jesus the King saying the hungry stood in for him; Muslims hear God's nearness to the sick, and hold that God never becomes one of his creatures.' Confirm both halves are fair, and that nothing ranks or blends the two.
In the hadith's food and drink parts, the wording is that you would have found that (the reward) with God; the voice says only 'hunger and thirst come next, in the same pattern'. Confirm.
Who 'the least of these my brethren' are is given as a difference among Christian readers. Confirm the wording is fair.
The sentence of the goats (25:41, 46) is not retold. Confirm the omission is acceptable.
howItsDone: the corporal works of mercy (Catholic teaching) come from this list plus burying the dead. Confirm.
